blocks.text: 31.13.4 Filters
blocks.raw_html: 31.13.4 Filters

blocks.text: Wavetable’s filters can be very useful for shaping the sonically rich timbres created by the oscillators and their effects. And, since the oscillators also provide you with the classic waveforms of analog synthesizers, you can very easily build a subtractive-style synthesizer with them.
blocks.raw_html: Wavetable’s filters can be very useful for shaping the sonically rich timbres created by the oscillators and their effects. And, since the oscillators also provide you with the classic waveforms of analog synthesizers, you can very easily build a subtractive-style synthesizer with them.

blocks.text: Wavetable offers a variety of filter types including low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, notch, and a special Morph filter. Each filter can be switched between 12 and 24 dB slopes as well as a selection of analog-modeled circuit behaviors developed in conjunction with Cytomic that emulate hardware filters found on some classic analog synthesizers.
blocks.raw_html: Wavetable offers a variety of filter types including low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, notch, and a special Morph filter. Each filter can be switched between 12 and 24 dB slopes as well as a selection of analog-modeled circuit behaviors developed in conjunction with Cytomic that emulate hardware filters found on some classic analog synthesizers.

blocks.text: The Clean circuit option is a high-quality, CPU-efficient design that is the same as the filters used in EQ Eight. This is available for all of the filter types.
blocks.raw_html: The Clean circuit option is a high-quality, CPU-efficient design that is the same as the filters used in EQ Eight. This is available for all of the filter types.

blocks.text: The OSR circuit option is a state-variable type with resonance limited by a unique hard-clipping diode. This is modeled on the filters used in a somewhat rare British monosynth, and is available for all filter types.
blocks.raw_html: The OSR circuit option is a state-variable type with resonance limited by a unique hard-clipping diode. This is modeled on the filters used in a somewhat rare British monosynth, and is available for all filter types.

blocks.text: The MS2 circuit option uses a Sallen-Key design and soft clipping to limit resonance. It is modeled on the filters used in a famous semi-modular Japanese monosynth and is available for the low-pass and high-pass filters.
blocks.raw_html: The MS2 circuit option uses a Sallen-Key design and soft clipping to limit resonance. It is modeled on the filters used in a famous semi-modular Japanese monosynth and is available for the low-pass and high-pass filters.

blocks.text: The SMP circuit is a custom design not based on any particular hardware. It shares characteristics of both the MS2 and PRD circuits and is available for the low-pass and high-pass filters.
blocks.raw_html: The SMP circuit is a custom design not based on any particular hardware. It shares characteristics of both the MS2 and PRD circuits and is available for the low-pass and high-pass filters.

blocks.text: The PRD circuit uses a ladder design and has no explicit resonance limiting. It is modeled on the filters used in a legacy dual-oscillator monosynth from the United States and is available for the low-pass and high-pass filters.
blocks.raw_html: The PRD circuit uses a ladder design and has no explicit resonance limiting. It is modeled on the filters used in a legacy dual-oscillator monosynth from the United States and is available for the low-pass and high-pass filters.

blocks.text: The most important filter parameters are the typical synth controls Frequency and Resonance. Frequency determines where in the harmonic spectrum the filter is applied; Resonance boosts frequencies near that point. Note that you can adjust the Frequency and Resonance parameters by clicking and dragging either of the filter dots in the filter display.
blocks.raw_html: The most important filter parameters are the typical synth controls Frequency and Resonance. Frequency determines where in the harmonic spectrum the filter is applied; Resonance boosts frequencies near that point. Note that you can adjust the Frequency and Resonance parameters by clicking and dragging either of the filter dots in the filter display.

blocks.text: When using the low-pass, high-pass, or band-pass filter with any circuit type besides Clean, there is an additional Drive control that can be used to add gain or distortion to the signal before it enters the filter.
blocks.raw_html: When using the low-pass, high-pass, or band-pass filter with any circuit type besides Clean, there is an additional Drive control that can be used to add gain or distortion to the signal before it enters the filter.

blocks.text: The Morph filter has an additional Morph control which sweeps the filter type continuously from low-pass to band-pass to high-pass to notch and back to low-pass.
blocks.raw_html: The Morph filter has an additional Morph control which sweeps the filter type continuously from low-pass to band-pass to high-pass to notch and back to low-pass.

blocks.text: Filter routing allows you to arrange the filters in various configurations for drastically different sculpting techniques. You can choose from one of three different routings:
blocks.raw_html: Filter routing allows you to arrange the filters in various configurations for drastically different sculpting techniques. You can choose from one of three different routings:

blocks.text: Serial — Routes all oscillators into Filter 1, and routes Filter 1 into Filter 2. Sub is routed to both filters.
blocks.raw_html: • Serial — Routes all oscillators into Filter 1, and routes Filter 1 into Filter 2. Sub is routed to both filters.

blocks.text: Parallel — Routes the two main oscillators into Filter 1 and Filter 2. Sub is routed to both filters.
blocks.raw_html: • Parallel — Routes the two main oscillators into Filter 1 and Filter 2. Sub is routed to both filters.

blocks.text: Split — Routes Oscillator 1 to Filter 1, and Oscillator 2 to Filter 2. Sub is split in half and sent to both filters. If either filter is off, the corresponding oscillator’s signal is still audible. Split can be used to treat each filter separately, and is useful for cases where you want to create layered synth sounds. If the main oscillators are disabled while both filters are engaged, Split can also be used to add extra treatment to the Sub oscillator.
blocks.raw_html: • Split — Routes Oscillator 1 to Filter 1, and Oscillator 2 to Filter 2. Sub is split in half and sent to both filters. If either filter is off, the corresponding oscillator’s signal is still audible. Split can be used to treat each filter separately, and is useful for cases where you want to create layered synth sounds. If the main oscillators are disabled while both filters are engaged, Split can also be used to add extra treatment to the Sub oscillator.

blocks.text: 31.13.5 Matrix Tab
blocks.raw_html: 31.13.5 Matrix Tab

blocks.text: The Modulation Matrix enables assigning modulation from Envelopes and LFOs (also known as “internal modulation sources”) to parameters within the instrument (or “modulation targets”).
blocks.raw_html: The Modulation Matrix enables assigning modulation from Envelopes and LFOs (also known as “internal modulation sources”) to parameters within the instrument (or “modulation targets”).

blocks.text: The modulation sources run horizontally, while the modulation targets run vertically. Click and drag within the grid to change the amount of modulation that the selected source applies to the selected parameter.
blocks.raw_html: The modulation sources run horizontally, while the modulation targets run vertically. Click and drag within the grid to change the amount of modulation that the selected source applies to the selected parameter.

blocks.text: Note that certain parameters are additive modulation targets, while others are multiplicative modulation targets.
blocks.raw_html: Note that certain parameters are additive modulation targets, while others are multiplicative modulation targets.

blocks.text: Additive modulation is applied to a parameter using the following formula:
blocks.raw_html: Additive modulation is applied to a parameter using the following formula:

blocks.text: The outputs of a parameter’s modulation sources are summed together.
blocks.raw_html: • The outputs of a parameter’s modulation sources are summed together.

blocks.text: The summed modulation value is added to the current parameter value.
blocks.raw_html: • The summed modulation value is added to the current parameter value.

blocks.text: Modulation values for additive modulation are centered around 0, with 0 being the “neutral” value. Additive modulation values can be negative or positive. Modulation sources that output negative and positive values are “bipolar” sources. Modulation sources that only output positive values are “unipolar” sources.
blocks.raw_html: Modulation values for additive modulation are centered around 0, with 0 being the “neutral” value. Additive modulation values can be negative or positive. Modulation sources that output negative and positive values are “bipolar” sources. Modulation sources that only output positive values are “unipolar” sources.

blocks.text: Multiplicative modulation is applied to a parameter using the following formula:
blocks.raw_html: Multiplicative modulation is applied to a parameter using the following formula:

blocks.text: The outputs of a parameter’s modulation sources are multiplied together.
blocks.raw_html: • The outputs of a parameter’s modulation sources are multiplied together.

blocks.text: The multiplied modulation value is multiplied with the current parameter value.
blocks.raw_html: • The multiplied modulation value is multiplied with the current parameter value.

blocks.text: The neutral value for multiplicative modulation is 1, and the minimum value is 0. Parameters with multiplicative modulation are noted throughout the Wavetable manual.
blocks.raw_html: The neutral value for multiplicative modulation is 1, and the minimum value is 0. Parameters with multiplicative modulation are noted throughout the Wavetable manual.

blocks.text: Click on a parameter in the instrument to make it appear temporarily in the matrix. If you apply modulation to this parameter, it will remain in the matrix. If no modulation is applied, the parameter will disappear from the matrix when you click another parameter. Note that the Matrix tab and MIDI tab share the same rows.
blocks.raw_html: Click on a parameter in the instrument to make it appear temporarily in the matrix. If you apply modulation to this parameter, it will remain in the matrix. If no modulation is applied, the parameter will disappear from the matrix when you click another parameter. Note that the Matrix tab and MIDI tab share the same rows.

blocks.text: Click on any of the modulation source headers located above the matrix to quickly jump to its respective panel within the Mod Sources tab.
blocks.raw_html: Click on any of the modulation source headers located above the matrix to quickly jump to its respective panel within the Mod Sources tab.

blocks.text: The Time slider will scale the times of all the modulators. Negative values will make envelopes and LFOs faster, while positive values will make them slower. Modulating this value with an envelope or LFO will not affect the assigned modulator, but that modulator will still scale to other destinations.
blocks.raw_html: The Time slider will scale the times of all the modulators. Negative values will make envelopes and LFOs faster, while positive values will make them slower. Modulating this value with an envelope or LFO will not affect the assigned modulator, but that modulator will still scale to other destinations.

blocks.text: The Amount slider sets the overall amount of modulation for all sources in the modulation matrix. Note that this is a multiplicative modulation destination.
blocks.raw_html: The Amount slider sets the overall amount of modulation for all sources in the modulation matrix. Note that this is a multiplicative modulation destination.

blocks.text: 31.13.6 Mod Sources Tab
blocks.raw_html: 31.13.6 Mod Sources Tab

blocks.text: The Mod Sources tab allows you to adjust Envelope and LFO settings, which are described in more detail below.
blocks.raw_html: The Mod Sources tab allows you to adjust Envelope and LFO settings, which are described in more detail below.

blocks.text: Envelopes
blocks.raw_html: Envelopes

blocks.text: Wavetable’s envelopes (Amp, Env 2 and Env 3) can be modified using Time and Slope parameters, while Env 2 and Env 3 include additional Value controls. Note that you can adjust the Time, Slope and Value parameters by clicking and dragging the envelope display.
blocks.raw_html: Wavetable’s envelopes (Amp, Env 2 and Env 3) can be modified using Time and Slope parameters, while Env 2 and Env 3 include additional Value controls. Note that you can adjust the Time, Slope and Value parameters by clicking and dragging the envelope display.

blocks.text: Attack sets the time needed to travel from the initial value to the Peak value. The shape of this stage of the envelope is determined by the Attack Slope value.
blocks.raw_html: Attack sets the time needed to travel from the initial value to the Peak value. The shape of this stage of the envelope is determined by the Attack Slope value.

blocks.text: Decay sets the time needed to travel from the Peak value to the Sustain level. The shape of this stage of the envelope is determined by the Decay Slope value.
blocks.raw_html: Decay sets the time needed to travel from the Peak value to the Sustain level. The shape of this stage of the envelope is determined by the Decay Slope value.

blocks.text: Sustain sets the level reached at the end of the Decay stage. The envelope will remain at this level until a Note Off occurs, unless the Loop mode is set to Trigger or Loop, in which case it will continue to the Release stage as soon as it is reached. Note that this is a multiplicative modulation destination.
blocks.raw_html: Sustain sets the level reached at the end of the Decay stage. The envelope will remain at this level until a Note Off occurs, unless the Loop mode is set to Trigger or Loop, in which case it will continue to the Release stage as soon as it is reached. Note that this is a multiplicative modulation destination.

blocks.text: Release sets the time needed to travel to the Final value after a Note Off occurs. The shape of this stage of the envelope is determined by the Release Slope value.
blocks.raw_html: Release sets the time needed to travel to the Final value after a Note Off occurs. The shape of this stage of the envelope is determined by the Release Slope value.

blocks.text: As mentioned above, Wavetable’s envelopes also provide parameters that adjust the slope of their envelope segments. Positive slope values cause the envelope to move quickly at the beginning, then slower. Negative slope values cause the envelope to remain flat for longer, then move faster at the end. A slope of zero is linear; the envelope will move at the same rate throughout the segment.
blocks.raw_html: As mentioned above, Wavetable’s envelopes also provide parameters that adjust the slope of their envelope segments. Positive slope values cause the envelope to move quickly at the beginning, then slower. Negative slope values cause the envelope to remain flat for longer, then move faster at the end. A slope of zero is linear; the envelope will move at the same rate throughout the segment.

blocks.text: The Initial slider sets the starting value of the envelope when it is triggered. Note that this is a multiplicative modulation destination. This control is not available for the amp envelope.
blocks.raw_html: The Initial slider sets the starting value of the envelope when it is triggered. Note that this is a multiplicative modulation destination. This control is not available for the amp envelope.

blocks.text: The Peak slider sets the value which marks the end of the Attack stage and the beginning of the Decay stage. This control is not available for the amp envelope.
blocks.raw_html: The Peak slider sets the value which marks the end of the Attack stage and the beginning of the Decay stage. This control is not available for the amp envelope.

blocks.text: The Final slider sets the value at the end of the Release stage. This control is not available for the amp envelope.
blocks.raw_html: The Final slider sets the value at the end of the Release stage. This control is not available for the amp envelope.

blocks.text: The Loop Modes drop-down lets you choose from one of three modes:
blocks.raw_html: The Loop Modes drop-down lets you choose from one of three modes:

blocks.text: None will hold the Sustain portion until a Note Off, and will not loop.
blocks.raw_html: • None will hold the Sustain portion until a Note Off, and will not loop.

blocks.text: Trigger will play all segments once a Note On is received.
blocks.raw_html: • Trigger will play all segments once a Note On is received.

blocks.text: Loop will loop the entire envelope without holding the Sustain, until the voice ends.
blocks.raw_html: • Loop will loop the entire envelope without holding the Sustain, until the voice ends.
31.13.6.1 LFOs

blocks.text: Wavetable includes two LFOs, which can be adjusted individually via the parameters described in this section.
blocks.raw_html: Wavetable includes two LFOs, which can be adjusted individually via the parameters described in this section.

blocks.text: You can choose from one of five LFO waveforms, and use the Shape slider to modify the selected waveform’s shape:
blocks.raw_html: You can choose from one of five LFO waveforms, and use the Shape slider to modify the selected waveform’s shape:

blocks.text: Sine and Saw: Applies an increasing or decreasing slope.
blocks.raw_html: • Sine and Saw: Applies an increasing or decreasing slope.

blocks.text: Triangle: Morphs the symmetry from Ramp to Saw, with Triangle in the middle.
blocks.raw_html: • Triangle: Morphs the symmetry from Ramp to Saw, with Triangle in the middle.

blocks.text: Square: Changes the pulse width.
blocks.raw_html: • Square: Changes the pulse width.

blocks.text: Random: Changes the distribution of extreme values.
blocks.raw_html: • Random: Changes the distribution of extreme values.

blocks.text: The Sync switch sets the LFO Rate in Hertz or synced to the song tempo, while the Rate slider sets the LFO frequency in Hertz or beat divisions. Note that you can also adjust the LFO frequency by dragging the waveform display.
blocks.raw_html: The Sync switch sets the LFO Rate in Hertz or synced to the song tempo, while the Rate slider sets the LFO frequency in Hertz or beat divisions. Note that you can also adjust the LFO frequency by dragging the waveform display.

blocks.text: Amount adjusts the amount of LFO modulation that is applied to incoming signals. Note that this is a multiplicative modulation destination.
blocks.raw_html: Amount adjusts the amount of LFO modulation that is applied to incoming signals. Note that this is a multiplicative modulation destination.

blocks.text: The Offset slider offsets the phase of the LFO so that it starts at a different value. Note that Offset cannot be modulated.
blocks.raw_html: The Offset slider offsets the phase of the LFO so that it starts at a different value. Note that Offset cannot be modulated.

blocks.text: You can use the LFO Attack slider to adjust the time the LFO takes to fade in, when it has been triggered by a Note On.
blocks.raw_html: You can use the LFO Attack slider to adjust the time the LFO takes to fade in, when it has been triggered by a Note On.

blocks.text: When enabled, the LFO Retrigger switch will cause the LFO to reset to its starting point, or initial phase, on each new MIDI note. This can create hybrid LFO shapes if the LFO is retriggered before completing a cycle.
blocks.raw_html: When enabled, the LFO Retrigger switch will cause the LFO to reset to its starting point, or initial phase, on each new MIDI note. This can create hybrid LFO shapes if the LFO is retriggered before completing a cycle.

blocks.text: 31.13.7 MIDI Tab
blocks.raw_html: 31.13.7 MIDI Tab

blocks.text: Assigning MIDI to parameters can turn Wavetable into a dynamic performance instrument. Within the MIDI Modulation Matrix, MIDI modulation sources can be assigned to multiple parameters within the instrument (or “modulation targets”).
blocks.raw_html: Assigning MIDI to parameters can turn Wavetable into a dynamic performance instrument. Within the MIDI Modulation Matrix, MIDI modulation sources can be assigned to multiple parameters within the instrument (or “modulation targets”).

blocks.text: When Velocity is assigned, Wavetable will use the incoming MIDI note’s velocity value to modulate target parameters for the duration of that note.
blocks.raw_html: When Velocity is assigned, Wavetable will use the incoming MIDI note’s velocity value to modulate target parameters for the duration of that note.

blocks.text: When Note is assigned, Wavetable will use the incoming MIDI note’s pitch to modulate target parameters for the duration of that note. The pitch modulation range is centered around C3. This means when it is assigned to Filter Frequency with the modulation amount set to 100%, the filter will precisely track the played note.
blocks.raw_html: When Note is assigned, Wavetable will use the incoming MIDI note’s pitch to modulate target parameters for the duration of that note. The pitch modulation range is centered around C3. This means when it is assigned to Filter Frequency with the modulation amount set to 100%, the filter will precisely track the played note.

blocks.text: Pitch Bend, Aftertouch and Modulation Wheel: these are hardware controls found on many MIDI controller devices. If you do not have such a device, you can still modulate the parameters with clip envelopes.
blocks.raw_html: Pitch Bend, Aftertouch and Modulation Wheel: these are hardware controls found on many MIDI controller devices. If you do not have such a device, you can still modulate the parameters with clip envelopes.

blocks.text: When Random is assigned, Wavetable will modulate target parameters by a random value, which is calculated each time a note is triggered.
blocks.raw_html: When Random is assigned, Wavetable will modulate target parameters by a random value, which is calculated each time a note is triggered.

blocks.text: Click on a parameter in the instrument to make it appear temporarily in the matrix. If you apply modulation to this parameter, it will remain in the matrix. If no modulation is applied, the parameter will disappear from the matrix when you click another parameter. Note that the Matrix tab and MIDI tab share the same rows.
blocks.raw_html: Click on a parameter in the instrument to make it appear temporarily in the matrix. If you apply modulation to this parameter, it will remain in the matrix. If no modulation is applied, the parameter will disappear from the matrix when you click another parameter. Note that the Matrix tab and MIDI tab share the same rows.

blocks.text: 31.13.8 Global and Unison Controls
blocks.raw_html: 31.13.8 Global and Unison Controls

blocks.text: Wavetable’s global controls affect the overall behavior and performance of the instrument.
blocks.raw_html: Wavetable’s global controls affect the overall behavior and performance of the instrument.

blocks.text: Transpose adjusts the relative pitch of the Wavetable instrument in semitones.
blocks.raw_html: Transpose adjusts the relative pitch of the Wavetable instrument in semitones.

blocks.text: Volume adjusts the overall level of the instrument. Note that is a multiplicative modulation destination.
blocks.raw_html: Volume adjusts the overall level of the instrument. Note that is a multiplicative modulation destination.

blocks.text: The Poly/Mono toggle switches the instrument between a single voice with legato envelopes (Mono) and a polyphonic instrument (Poly).
blocks.raw_html: The Poly/Mono toggle switches the instrument between a single voice with legato envelopes (Mono) and a polyphonic instrument (Poly).

blocks.text: The Poly Voices drop-down menu lets you set the maximum number of notes that can sound simultaneously. Note that Poly Voices is only active when the Poly/Mono switch is set to Poly.
blocks.raw_html: The Poly Voices drop-down menu lets you set the maximum number of notes that can sound simultaneously. Note that Poly Voices is only active when the Poly/Mono switch is set to Poly.

blocks.text: Glide adjusts the time overlapping notes take to slide their pitch to the next incoming pitch. Note that Glide is only active when the Poly/Mono switch is set to Mono.
blocks.raw_html: Glide adjusts the time overlapping notes take to slide their pitch to the next incoming pitch. Note that Glide is only active when the Poly/Mono switch is set to Mono.

blocks.text: The Unison drop-down menu lets you choose from one of six unison modes (or none). Unison modes use multiple oscillators with different phases, stereo locations, or wavetable positions to provide a fuller sound.
blocks.raw_html: The Unison drop-down menu lets you choose from one of six unison modes (or none). Unison modes use multiple oscillators with different phases, stereo locations, or wavetable positions to provide a fuller sound.

blocks.text: Classic: The oscillators are detuned with equal spacing and panned to alternating stereo channels.
blocks.raw_html: • Classic: The oscillators are detuned with equal spacing and panned to alternating stereo channels.

blocks.text: Shimmer: The oscillator pitches are jittered at random intervals, giving a shimmering reverb-like effect. A small amount of wavetable offset is also applied for extra fullness.
blocks.raw_html: • Shimmer: The oscillator pitches are jittered at random intervals, giving a shimmering reverb-like effect. A small amount of wavetable offset is also applied for extra fullness.

blocks.text: Noise: Pitches are jittered as in the Shimmer unison mode, but at a much faster rate, resulting in noisy breathy textures. A small amount of wavetable offset is applied for extra fullness.
blocks.raw_html: • Noise: Pitches are jittered as in the Shimmer unison mode, but at a much faster rate, resulting in noisy breathy textures. A small amount of wavetable offset is applied for extra fullness.

blocks.text: Phase Sync: The oscillators are detuned as in Classic unison mode, but the phases are synced when a note is started giving a strong sweeping phaser-style effect.
blocks.raw_html: • Phase Sync: The oscillators are detuned as in Classic unison mode, but the phases are synced when a note is started giving a strong sweeping phaser-style effect.

blocks.text: Position spread: The wavetable positions for each oscillator are evenly spread out by an amount. A small amount of detune is additionally applied for extra width.
blocks.raw_html: • Position spread: The wavetable positions for each oscillator are evenly spread out by an amount. A small amount of detune is additionally applied for extra width.

blocks.text: Random note: The wavetable positions and detune amount for each oscillator are randomised each time a note is started.
blocks.raw_html: • Random note: The wavetable positions and detune amount for each oscillator are randomised each time a note is started.

blocks.text: The Voices slider sets the number of simultaneously running oscillators per wavetable oscillator. More voices will result in a thicker sound, whereas less voices will sound clearer.
blocks.raw_html: The Voices slider sets the number of simultaneously running oscillators per wavetable oscillator. More voices will result in a thicker sound, whereas less voices will sound clearer.

blocks.text: The Amount slider adjusts the intensity of the unison effect, and has different behavior in each unison mode. Note that this is a multiplicative modulation destination.
blocks.raw_html: The Amount slider adjusts the intensity of the unison effect, and has different behavior in each unison mode. Note that this is a multiplicative modulation destination.

blocks.text: 31.13.9 Hi-Quality Mode
blocks.raw_html: 31.13.9 Hi-Quality Mode

blocks.text: You can toggle on Hi-Quality mode on or off from Wavetable’s context menu.
blocks.raw_html: You can toggle on Hi-Quality mode on or off from Wavetable’s context menu.

blocks.text: When Hi-Quality is off, Wavetable modulation is calculated every 32 samples. Low-power versions of the Cytomic filters are also used to further reduce CPU.
blocks.raw_html: When Hi-Quality is off, Wavetable modulation is calculated every 32 samples. Low-power versions of the Cytomic filters are also used to further reduce CPU.

blocks.text: Using Wavetable with Hi-Quality mode off can save up to 25% CPU compared to having it enabled, which is ideal for working with large sets or maintaining low latencies.
blocks.raw_html: Using Wavetable with Hi-Quality mode off can save up to 25% CPU compared to having it enabled, which is ideal for working with large sets or maintaining low latencies.

blocks.text: As of Live 11.1, Hi-Quality mode will be off by default when loading a new instance of Wavetable or any of its Core Library presets. However, any user presets or Live Sets created previously will still load Wavetable in Hi-Quality mode to ensure sound consistency with earlier Live versions.
blocks.raw_html: As of Live 11.1, Hi-Quality mode will be off by default when loading a new instance of Wavetable or any of its Core Library presets. However, any user presets or Live Sets created previously will still load Wavetable in Hi-Quality mode to ensure sound consistency with earlier Live versions.

blocks.text: Note: Subtle sound differences may occur when Hi-Quality mode is enabled.
blocks.raw_html: Note: Subtle sound differences may occur when Hi-Quality mode is enabled.

owner_requirements.contract: Osc 1 offers Sine, Triangle, Shark Tooth, Saturated, Saw, Pulse and Rectangle; Osc 2 offers Sine, Triangle, Saturated, Saw and Rectangle.
Osc 1 Oct transposes octaves and Shape changes its waveform display; Osc 2 Oct transposes octaves and Detune uses semitones. Combined display includes enabled oscillator/noise output.

Osc 1 Shape sources are Env 1, Env 2/Cyc, LFO, Key, Velocity, Modwheel, Pressure and Slide. Shape Mod Amount spans -100% to 100%; positive Shape Mod can act even with Shape 0%. Key modulation reverses direction with amount sign.
Two pitch modulation sources affect both oscillators, each with amount -100% to 100%; Ratio-mode LFO pitch modulation is documented as able to produce FM tones.
Osc 1, Osc 2 and white-noise generator have independent enables/gains and individual filter-routing arrows. Routing off bypasses the filter for that source.
The manual describes oscillator gain -6 dB and saturation changes above 0 dB in the filter path; it supplies no transfer curve or measured thresholds for this build.
Oscillator R on resets both oscillator phases at each note; R off is free-running.

Low-pass Type I is labelled 12 dB/octave and Type II 24 dB/octave. Freq/Res and high-pass HP are separate; display dots adjust HP horizontally and LP frequency/resonance horizontally/vertically. Key 0.00 disables note influence on LP frequency; 1.00 follows note direction.
Two independent low-pass cutoff modulation slots each have amount -100% to 100%.

Envelope 1 controls amplitude of both oscillators and noise; Attack reaches peak, Decay reaches Sustain, Sustain holds until note ends, Release returns to zero. Knobs/display and 1/2 selectors edit the selected envelope.
Env 2 is a modulation source and can switch ADSR to Cycling; Cycling restarts on each MIDI note, offers Tilt/Hold and Rate/Ratio/Time/Sync using Hz/ratio/ms/beat divisions.

LFO time modes are Rate, Ratio, Time and Sync. Nine waveforms include Sine, Triangle, Saw Up/Down, Square, Sample & Hold, Wander, Linear Envelope and Exponential Envelope. R resets per note; off free-runs; Amount and its modulation source/depth control intensity.

Mod section has up to three source/destination slots with -100% to 100% amount. Sources are Env 1, Env 2/Cyc, LFO, Key, Velocity, Modwheel, Pressure, Slide; destinations include oscillator gains/shape/detune, Noise Gain, LP Frequency/Resonance, HP Frequency, LFO/Cyc rate and Main Volume.

Voice modes Poly, Mono, Stereo and Unison use respectively one, up to four, two and four voices per note. At Voices 32, Poly/Stereo/Unison permit 32/16/8 notes. Mono Thickness 0 uses one audible voice; new held-note onset chokes the previous note.
Drift changes per-voice oscillator and filter variation; no seed, distribution, repeatability or exact zero-variation law is supplied.
Mono Legato allows a new held-overlap note to change pitch without restarting envelopes; Glide sets overlapping-note pitch-slide time.
Volume and Vel > Vol control output/velocity; Transpose spans -48 to +48 semitones. Note PB toggles per-note pitch bend independently of global PB Range.

Browser double-click or waveform drag/drop loads a sample. Start and Length use percentages of total sample length; Shift-drag Start gives fine adjustment and waveform zoom. Start/Length/Gain update the display.
Sample Gain spans -70 to +24 dB, Transpose -48 to +48 semitones, Detune -50 to +50 cents, global Volume -36 to +36 dB. Pan changes stereo position and Velocity to Volume controls velocity response.
Trigger uses Attack/Hold/Decay and continues through Hold after note release; Hold inf plays the full sample. Gate disables Hold and starts Decay at note release.

Next/Previous Similar Sample cycle related samples; Show Similar Files opens browser results; Return to Reference returns to initial reference and Save as Similarity Reference replaces it. Waveform hot-swap replaces sample; title hot-swap replaces instrument.
Playback Effect On gates nine choices: Stretch, Loop, Pitch Env, Punch, 8-Bit, FM, Ring Mod, Sub Osc and Noise. Each has two controls; X/Y vertical edits first, horizontal second.
Stretch changes sample length without intended pitch change; Factor is a speed multiple and Grain Size uses milliseconds. Exact grain/window/interpolation law is unknown.
Loop repeats a sample region; Loop Offset is relative to sample start and Loop Length is milliseconds.
Pitch Env Amount -100% to +100% sets signed pitch change and Decay returns to base pitch defined by global controls.
Punch applies transient ducking; Amount controls reduction and Release controls return to zero gain reduction. Exact attack/envelope law is unknown.
8-Bit offers Sample Rate and Decay Time for its low-pass behavior; no bit-depth/aliasing/kernel equivalence follows from the name.

FM modulates sample pitch with a sine; Ring Mod modulates amplitude with low-rate tremolo and higher-rate ring-modulation character. Both have Amount/Frequency and modulation decay follows global Decay.
Sub Osc and Noise layer a generator following device Attack/Decay. Sub Frequency spans 30-120 Hz; Noise Color filters noise.
Time/frequency controls of Stretch, Loop, FM, Ring Mod, Sub Osc and Noise follow global pitch and played MIDI pitch; exact scaling is not supplied.
Filter On gates four types: 12 dB LP, 24 dB LP, 24 dB HP and Peak. LP/HP expose Resonance/Frequency; Peak exposes Peak Gain/Frequency.
Mod source is Velocity or Slide (MPE); destinations are Filter, Attack, Hold, Decay, FX1 and FX2. FX1/FX2 address current effect controls; amount controls depth.
Enable Per-Note Pitch Bend is documented enabled by default. Envelope Follows Pitch scales envelope relative to sample pitch so it affects the same portion when transposed.
Drum Sampler > Simpler replaces the instrument retaining sample Start and Length positions; other parameter translations are not established.
Save as Default Pad from a Drum Rack pad context makes new samples on empty pads load Drum Sampler.
Expanded View reveals all modulation sources/targets; A/B selects engine matrix, Copy to A/B copies modulation values and X clears active modulation values.
Engines A/B enable independently. Disabling an engine deactivates its filter; a filter can be disabled without disabling its engine.
Engine Octaves/Semitones/Cents pitch controls become scale-degree transposition when Use Current Scale follows Live Scale Mode; Pitch Quant target is included.

Oscillator macros depend on selected type: Basic Shapes Shape/Tone; Dual Basic Shapes Shape/Detune; Noisy Shapes Shape/Rough; Square Sync Freq 1/2; Square 5th 5th Amt/P Width; Sub Tone/Aux; four Swarms Motion/Spacing; Harmonic Fm Amount/Ratio; Fold Fm Amount/Shape; Squelch Amount/Feedback; Simple Fm Amount/Ratio; Chip Tone/Rate. Overview type count is unresolved.
Shepard’s Pi Rate 0.0-49.9 descends, 50.0 has no movement, 50.1-100.0 ascends; Width changes octave count.

Remaining described macros are Tarp Decay/Tone; Extratone Pitch/Env Amount; Noise Loop Rate/Fade; Filtered Noise Freq/Width; Bitgrunge Freq/Mult; Crackle Density/Intensity; Rain Tone/Rate; Bubble Density/Spread; Chord Shape/Inversion. Named descriptions do not prove kernels or RNG.

Chord uses four sawtooth oscillators with Shape intervals and Inversion order. With Use Current Scale, chords use selected scale; with no scale set, incoming root uses major. Availability/version/context remains unresolved.

Amp/Mod envelopes offer ADSR and slopes; Trigger plays all segments ignoring Sustain, Loop repeats entire envelope without holding Sustain, AD Loop repeats Attack/Decay. Mod envelope adds Initial/Peak/Final.
Link Envelopes links corresponding engine Amplitude and Modulation envelopes.

Each engine has LFO 1 and 2 with Hz/sync, Phase Offset and Retrigger. LFO 1 types are Basic Shapes, Ramp, Wander, Alternate, Euclid, Pulsate; FX1/2 each describe eighteen serial effects. LFO 1 and processed LFO1 FX are separate sources. LFO 2 offers Sine, Tri, Saw Up/Down, Rectangle, Random S&H.

Matrix source columns/target rows accept signed modulation. Clicking parameter adds it to selected engine matrix; unmodulated temporary row disappears on next selection. Additive/multiplicative target assignment and complete units remain U.

Velocity and Pitch sources use note values for that note duration; Random gets new value at note trigger. MIDI Pitch Bend/Press/Wheel and MPE Note Pitch Bend/Slide/Press supply sources, including clip envelopes.
Osc Key Tracking off produces C3 constant pitch, or scale root in C3 octave when scale mode active; on follows incoming note.
Phase Reset enables Phase Spread. With Reset on, Spread off sets start phase zero; Spread on follows Spread matrix source.

Oscillator Scale Awareness lists Dual Basic Shapes, Swarm Sine/Triangle/Saw/Square and Chip. Filter Scale Awareness lists Plate and Membrane Resonators. These per-engine settings are distinct from Use Current Scale.
Portamento slides continuously and Glissando in discrete steps, using scale degrees when scale awareness is on. Both Mono and Poly permit Glide, audible only with Glide Time above zero.

Filter types have Frequency and type-dependent macros. SVF 12/24 L-B-H-N morphs LP/BP/HP/notch; MS2 LP/HP, OSR BP, LP Crunch, LP Switched Res Lofi and Filther are described. Q emphasizes cutoff and Drive saturates input.
Eq Peak Boost/width and Eq Notch Cut/width, Phaser Feedback/Spread, Redux Crush/Lofi, Vowel Morph and Comb +/- Feedback/Damp have distinct roles.
Plate and Membrane Resonators describe first 32 modes of rectangular plate/circular membrane and scale-following resonant frequencies with Filter Scale Awareness.
Per-engine Volume/Pan and Tone Filter are separate; positive Tone reduces lows and negative Tone reduces highs.
Mixer Drive is per voice after engine mixer settings and before per-voice limiter; Limit gates limiter after both engines mixed and global Drive applied. Global Volume sets output.
Mono permits Legato: overlap with Legato on reuses current envelope position, off restarts envelope. Poly exposes 2-12 voices.
Stacked Voices duplicates both engines including filters/modulation/mix. Spread offsets stacked voices, or notes in held chord when Stacked Voices Off. Spread has no effect without a matrix target.
The matrix paragraph says negative values speed envelopes/LFOs and positive slow them, but the applicable target/preconditions are unspecified; do not generalize that statement to all destinations.
Four oscillators use eleven predefined algorithms; icons describe top-to-bottom routing. Algorithm selector supports MIDI mapping, automation and real-time modulation.

Wave chooser includes sine, resynthesized saw/square/triangle variants, Sine 4/8 Bit, Saw D, Square D, Noise Looped, Noise White and User. Numeric harmonic names denote retained harmonic counts, not exact output samples.

Harmonics editor offers 16/32/64 partials, Shift constrains editing to one harmonic, Repeat off truncates above chosen count, even/odd/all drawing and Normalize; waveform copy/paste works across oscillators.
Waveform context exports .ams to User Library Samples/Waveforms; browser drag imports .ams into an oscillator; Simpler/Sampler are also documented consumers.

Osc Coarse/Fine set note-relative ratios; Fixed replaces controls with Frequency Hz and Multiplier and ignores note pitch, with described low endpoint 0.1 Hz. The manual states fixed frequency is Freq multiplied by Multi; no note-frequency formula is supplied.
Osc < Vel controls signed velocity pitch response; Q quantizes it as Coarse changes.
Each oscillator Level/envelope responds to Vel/Key; Phase and R control note-start phase/free-run. Feedback acts only on oscillators not modulated by another oscillator.

Antialias and Interpolation are independently selectable, Tone affects high-frequency content. Manual new-patch default Antialias on does not prove installed constructor/preset defaults or a numerical alias bound.

LFO routes Dest A to selected oscillators/filter and Dest B to one extra target; global Amount, Vel and envelope scale depths. Range Low describes 50 seconds-30 Hz, Hi 8 Hz-12 kHz and Sync tempo; R resets/free-runs; Rate < Key 100% doubles per octave.

Seven envelopes cover oscillators/filter/pitch/LFO; oscillator Attack is documented linear and Decay/Release exponential, ending -inf dB. Filter/pitch slopes and End vary. Note Off starts Release from current value. Shapes copy across oscillators.

Envelope modes include Loop, Beat, Sync and Trigger. Beat repeats note-relative without quantizing notes; Sync first repeat nearest sixteenth while song plays, otherwise Beat-like. Trigger ignores Note Off. Loop restart level is unresolved.

Loop restart wording differs: overview says current level to peak, Loop Time listing says sustain-to-initial then restart, Beat/Sync listing says current-to-peak. Applicability to the same mode/preconditions is unresolved.
Global Time, Time < Key and per-envelope Time < Vel scale envelope segments; Beat/Sync repetition beat-time is not changed by global Time or Time < Vel.
Pitch envelope can target A-D and LFO via Dest A and another Dest B; amount +100% follows levels and -100% inverts sign; envelope On gates it.

Filter types LP/HP/BP/notch/Morph offer 12/24 dB slopes. Clean/OSR apply all types; MS2/SMP/PRD LP/HP. Non-Clean LP/HP/BP expose Drive. Morph sweeps LP/BP/HP/notch and context snaps to named responses.
Filter Frequency responds to velocity/key/envelope/LFO; key 100% doubles per octave around C3. Play by Key sets Freq 466 Hz and Freq < Key 100%; this command is distinct from a global tuning formula.
Shaper chooser/Drive act on filtered path; Dry/Wet 0% bypasses shaper and shaper drive.

Voices supports up to 32; excess notes cut oldest notes. Voices 1 plays overlapping notes legato without retriggering envelopes. Global R retriggers an already enabled note rather than adding a voice.

Velocity, Key, Aftertouch, Pitch Bend and Mod Wheel each route to two targets with independent amounts; fixed Time < Key and PB Range coexist. Targets include Off, oscillator volume/crossfades/feedback/fixed pitch/FM Drive, filter controls, shaper, LFO, pitch envelope, Volume/Pan/Tone/Time; eligibility is target-specific.
Glide is polyphonic, starts new note at prior-note pitch then slides; legato Glide does not retrigger envelopes; Glide Time has no effect if Glide off.
Spread uses two detuned voices per note panned L/R; whether a note uses Spread is determined at Note On.
Transpose changes already-playing notes. Context commands copy oscillator parameters, set all envelope levels to maximum/minimum/middle, edit harmonics and export .ams.
Enable Per-Note Pitch Bend is documented on by default and can be disabled in device-title context.

Two oscillators enable independently; tabs select editing, expanded view redistributes controls. Gain/Pan/Semi/Detune are per oscillator. Category/table choosers and arrows traverse category boundaries.
Dropping WAV/AIFF on visualization imports it; choosers/arrows then browse its folder. Raw bypasses automatic sample preprocessing.
Dragging visualization or Wave Position selects table position. Linear/polar show same data with distinct layouts.

Oscillator effects are FM (Amt/Tune), Classic (PW/Sync), Modern (Warp/Fold). Two effect values persist across effect-type changes. FM Tune +/-50% and +/-100% describe +/-1 and +/-2 octave modulator offsets.
Sub enables independently with Gain, Tone 0% sine/increasing harmonics, and one/two octave-down switches relative to note/global Transpose.

Each filter offers LP/HP/BP/notch/Morph, 12/24 dB slopes; Clean/OSR all types and MS2/SMP/PRD LP/HP. Non-Clean LP/HP/BP expose Drive. Display dots adjust Frequency/Resonance; Morph traverses LP/BP/HP/notch.

Serial sends mains through Filter 1 then 2; Parallel feeds mains to both; Split assigns Osc 1/2 to Filter 1/2 and halves Sub to both. Split leaves corresponding oscillator audible when its filter is off.

Matrix uses source columns/target rows. Additive values sum then add to parameter, neutral 0; multiplicative values multiply then multiply parameter, neutral 1 minimum 0. Source units, depth scaling, clamps and each target assignment remain unresolved except explicit labels.
Clicked parameter appears temporarily; nonzero modulation keeps its row, otherwise next selected parameter replaces it. Matrix and MIDI tabs share rows; source headers jump to source panels.
Time scales all modulator times, negative faster/positive slower. A modulator assigned to Time does not scale itself through that route but still scales other destinations.
Global Matrix Amount, LFO Amount, instrument Volume and Unison Amount are documented multiplicative destinations.

Amp, Env2 and Env3 have Time/Slope; Env2/3 also Initial/Peak/Final, absent on Amp. Positive slopes start fast then slow; negative slow then fast; zero linear. Sustain/Initial are documented multiplicative where present.
Envelope None holds Sustain until Note Off; Trigger plays all segments at Note On; Loop repeats whole envelope without Sustain hold until voice ends.
Two LFOs offer Sine, Saw, Triangle, Square and Random with waveform-dependent Shape. Sync switches rate Hz/beat divisions.
LFO Offset sets start phase and cannot be modulated; Attack fades in after Note On; Retrigger resets phase on each new note.
MIDI Velocity/Note apply through note duration; Note 100% Filter Frequency tracks pitch around C3. Pitch Bend/Aftertouch/Wheel can use clip envelopes; Random samples at each new note.
Transpose uses semitones; Mono is single voice with legato envelopes and permits Glide; Poly enables Poly Voices and disables Glide.
Unison choices are none, Classic, Shimmer, Noise, Phase Sync, Position spread and Random note. They differ in detune, phase reset, stereo and position/randomization roles.
Unison Voices controls oscillators per main wavetable oscillator; Amount is mode-dependent intensity, distinct from Poly Voices note count.
Hi-Quality context switch controls quality; off is documented modulation every 32 samples and lower-power filters. CPU saving up to 25% is a conditional manual claim, not a required timing benchmark.

As of Live 11.1 the manual describes Hi-Quality off for new/Core Library instances while earlier user presets/Sets retain on for consistency; enabling may produce subtle differences. Migration boundaries for this target are unresolved.
Manual claims unmodulated raw oscillator output is band-limited with no aliasing at any pitch. No spectral measurement definition, finite pitch-domain fixture or tolerance accompanies this claim.

owner_fixtures.purpose: Finite future analyst setups, not executed reference fixtures or device defaults
common-setup: Editable test-owned Set; enabled isolated instrument on MIDI track; Monitor In; no later effects; track/master unmuted; output gain audible and attenuated; retain every displayed mode/value.

Analyst baseline: 4/4, 120 BPM, 48 kHz, host block 256; separated MIDI 60 velocity 96, beat 1 on/beat 3 off; overlap 48 on beat 1, 60 on beat 2, offs beats 3/4. All are stimulus choices, never product limits.

No sample file is fabricated by this author tool. Before media cases retain test-owned 2 s WAV sample A with distinct transient plus sustain and 1 s AIFF B, record bytes/rate/channels/hash. If unavailable case remains U.
Independent expression test uses two notes and separately identified per-note pitch/pressure/slide versus global pitch bend; exact transport codec remains with MPE owner.
positive-signal-guard: Enable oscillator/engine/sample and destination section, route source to audible output, set nonzero base gain, nonzero modulation/effect amount and nonzero stimulus; clear other routes and avoid mute/dry-only/zero-send baselines.

No-effect comparison first needs paired active positive baseline. Change only deliberate zero amount, disabled route, eligibility switch or ineligible target under test; never grade silence from an absent sample/note or inactive path.
Controls/state comparators inspect visible named state only. Acoustic adjectives, static package fields, defaults, CPU prose and names never substitute for retained output evidence.

assessments.quote: Drift is a versatile synthesizer with intuitive controls and a simple interface that is fully MPE-capable. Based on subtractive synthesis, Drift has been carefully built for quick and easy sound design while using minimal CPU resources.

assessments.quote: Drift’s interface is divided into six main sections: an oscillator section, a dynamic filter section, an envelopes section, two modulation sections (LFO and Mod), and a section of global controls.

assessments.quote: Subtractive synthesis is a technique that generally starts with a waveform that is then shaped using filters to sculpt the original timbres into new forms. In addition to this process, Drift offers many modulation options for tweaking and customizing the sound even more, allowing you to easily create a wide variety of sounds. The signature Drift control lets you add pitch and frequency variation to each voice, resulting in a slightly detuned, fluctuating pulse throughout the tone.

assessments.quote: You can select from several curated waveforms using the Osc 1 drop-down menu: Sine, Triangle, Shark Tooth, Saturated, Saw, Pulse, and Rectangle. The Shark Tooth and Saturated waveforms are unique to Drift; Shark Tooth is based on a classic Moog analog shape with the same name, while Saturated works well for bass sounds.

assessments.quote: The Oct knob transposes Oscillator 1 in octaves. You can use the Shape knob to change the harmonic content of the waveform into something slightly different, resulting in an effect similar to pulse-width modulation. As the timbre varies between each waveform, they all respond differently to the Shape control. When you make adjustments to the control, you can view the result in the Waveform Display located at the bottom of the Oscillator section. You’ll notice how the waveform changes as you tweak the Shape value.

assessments.quote: Meld is a versatile synthesizer that combines two independent macro oscillator engines into one device. While it can quickly dial in classic analog-style patches, Meld’s character shines through in the array of synthesis and filtering techniques it lets you layer and experiment with. Each of the device’s engines has a dedicated filter, envelopes, LFOs, and a MIDI and MPE-enabled Modulation Matrix, as well as two oscillator-dependent macro knobs that control parameters ranging from simple overtone modulation to more unusual features like noise loop fragmentation, chiptone pulsewidth, and raindrop generation density. Meld is designed to produce expressive, unfamiliar sounds guided by musical intention rather than technical detail.

assessments.quote: Meld’s dual-layer architecture can use up to two polyphonic synth engines at once. Its interface is divided into four main sections: the engines, the modulation section, the filters, and the global mix controls. This modular-inspired configuration makes it easy to add texture and movement to your sounds, but also to produce and capture musical surprises. To get familiar with some of Meld’s possibilities, try combining different waveform types and playing with each engine’s modulation macros. For more control, try mapping an engine’s parameters to its Modulation Matrix, or automating the device’s macro knobs using an LFO device. The more you experiment with the interaction between Meld’s two layers, the more you’ll make the device your own.

assessments.quote: Operator is an advanced and flexible synthesizer that combines the concept of “frequency modulation“ (FM) with classic subtractive and additive synthesis. It uses four multi-waveform oscillators that can modulate each other’s frequencies, creating very complex timbres from a limited number of objects. Operator includes a filter section, an LFO and global controls, as well as individual envelopes for the oscillators, filter, LFO and pitch.

assessments.quote: Typically, FM synthesis makes use of pure sine waves, creating more complex waveforms via modulation. However, in order to simplify sound design and to create a wider range of possible sounds, we designed Operator to produce a variety of other waveforms, including two types of noise. You can also draw your own waveforms via a partial editor. The instrument is made complete with an LFO, a pitch envelope and a filter section. Note that lots of “classic“ FM synthesizers create fantastic sounds without using filters at all, so we suggest exploring the possibilities of FM without the filter at first, and adding it later if necessary.

assessments.quote: The oscillators come with a built-in collection of basic waveform types — sine, sawtooth, square, triangle and noise — which are selected from the Wave chooser in the individual oscillator displays. The first of these waveforms is a pure, mathematical sine wave, which is usually the first choice for many FM timbres. We also added “Sine 4 Bit“ and “Sine 8 Bit“ to provide the retro sound adored by C64 fans, and “Saw D“ and “Square D“ digital waveforms, which are especially good for digital bass sounds. The square, triangle and sawtooth waveforms are resynthesized approximations of the ideal shape. The numbers included in the displayed name (e.g., “Square 6“) define how many harmonics are used for the resynthesis. Lower numbers sound mellower and are less likely to create aliasing when used on high pitches. There are also two built-in noise waveforms. The first, “Noise Looped,“ is a looping sample of noise. For truly random noise, choose “Noise White.“

assessments.quote: The frequency of an oscillator can be adjusted in the shell with its Coarse and Fine controls. An oscillator’s frequency usually follows that of played notes, but for some sounds it might be useful to set one or more oscillators to fixed frequencies. This can be done for each individual oscillator by activating the Fixed option. This allows the creation of sounds in which only the timbre will vary when different notes are played, but the tuning will stay the same. Fixed Mode would be useful, for example, in creating live drum sounds. Fixed Mode also allows producing very low frequencies down to 0.1 Hz. Note that when Fixed Mode is active, the frequency of the oscillator is controlled in the shell with the Frequency (Freq) and Multiplier (Multi) controls.

assessments.quote: Aliasing distortion is a common side effect of all digital synthesis and is the result of the finite sample rate and precision of digital systems. It mostly occurs at high frequencies. FM synthesis is especially likely to produce this kind of effect, since one can easily create sounds with lots of high harmonics. This also means that more complex oscillator waveforms, such as “Saw 32,“ tend to be more sensitive to aliasing than pure sine waves. Aliasing is a two-fold beast: A bit of it can be exactly what is needed to create a cool sound, yet a bit too much can make the timbre unplayable, as the perception of pitch is lost when high notes suddenly fold back into arbitrary pitches. Operator minimizes aliasing by working in a high-quality Antialias mode. This is on by default for new patches, but can be turned off in the global section. The Tone parameter in the global section also allows for controlling aliasing. Its effect is sometimes similar to a low-pass filter, but this depends on the nature of the sound itself and cannot generally be predicted. If you want to familiarize yourself with the sound of aliasing, turn Tone up fully and play a few very high notes. You will most likely notice that some notes sound completely different from other notes. Now, turn Tone down and the effect will be reduced, but the sound will be less bright.

assessments.quote: Each oscillator’s volume envelope is defined by six parameters: three rates and three levels. A rate is the time it takes to go from one level to the next. For instance, a typical pad sound starts with the initial level “-inf dB“ (which is silence), moves with an attack rate to its peak level, moves from there to the sustain level with a decay rate, and then finally, after Note Off occurs, back to “-inf dB“ at the release rate. Operator’s display provides a good overview of the actual shape of any particular envelope and lets you directly adjust the curve by clicking on a breakpoint and dragging. The breakpoints retain their selection after clicking, allowing them to be adjusted with the keyboard’s cursor keys, if desired.

assessments.quote: With FM synthesis, it is possible to create spectacular, endless, permuting sounds; the key to doing this is looping envelopes. Loop Mode can be activated in the lower left corner of the display. If an envelope in Operator is in Loop Mode and reaches sustain level while the note is still being held, it will be retriggered. The rate for this movement is defined by the Loop Time parameter. Note that envelopes in Loop Mode can loop very quickly and can therefore be used to achieve effects that one would not normally expect from an envelope generator.

assessments.quote: While Loop Mode is good for textures and experimental sounds, Operator also includes Beat and Sync Modes, which provide a simple way of creating rhythmical sounds. If set to Beat Mode, an envelope will restart after the beat time selected from the Repeat chooser. In Beat Mode, the repeat time is defined in fractions of song time, but notes are not quantized. If you play a note a bit out of sync, it will repeat perfectly but stay out of sync. In Sync Mode however, the first repetition is quantized to the nearest 16th note and, as a result, all following repetitions are synced to the song tempo. Note that Sync Mode only works if the song is playing, and otherwise it will behave like Beat Mode.

assessments.quote: Wavetable’s oscillators produce sound using a technique called wavetable synthesis. A wavetable is simply an arbitrary collection of short, looping samples that are arranged together. Playing a note with the oscillator fixed to just one of these samples will produce a steady tone with a consistent timbre. But the real power of wavetable synthesis comes by moving between the various samples in the table as the note plays, which results in a shifting timbre. Wavetable synthesis is extremely well-suited for producing dynamic sounds that change over time.

assessments.quote: FM — Applies frequency modulation to the oscillator. The Amt slider adjusts the intensity of the frequency modulation, while the Tune slider determines the frequency of the modulation oscillator. With a tuning of 50% (and -50%), the modulation oscillator is one octave higher (or lower) than the main oscillator. At 100% (and -100%), the modulation oscillator is two octaves higher (or lower). In between these values, the modulation oscillator is at inharmonic ratios, which is ideal for creating noisy overtones.

quotes.quote: With FM synthesis, it is possible to create spectacular, endless, permuting sounds; the key to doing this is looping envelopes. Loop Mode can be activated in the lower left corner of the display. If an envelope in Operator is in Loop Mode and reaches sustain level while the note is still being held, it will be retriggered. The rate for this movement is defined by the Loop Time parameter. Note that envelopes in Loop Mode can loop very quickly and can therefore be used to achieve effects that one would not normally expect from an envelope generator.

While Loop Mode is good for textures and experimental sounds, Operator also includes Beat and Sync Modes, which provide a simple way of creating rhythmical sounds. If set to Beat Mode, an envelope will restart after the beat time selected from the Repeat chooser. In Beat Mode, the repeat time is defined in fractions of song time, but notes are not quantized. If you play a note a bit out of sync, it will repeat perfectly but stay out of sync. In Sync Mode however, the first repetition is quantized to the nearest 16th note and, as a result, all following repetitions are synced to the song tempo. Note that Sync Mode only works if the song is playing, and otherwise it will behave like Beat Mode.
To avoid the audible clicks caused by restarting from its initial level, a looped envelope will restart from its actual level and move with the set attack rate to peak level.

Envelope Loop Mode (Loop) — If this is set to Loop, the envelope will start again after the end of the decay segment. If set to Beat or Sync, it will start again after a given beat-time. In Sync Mode, this behavior will be quantized to song time. In Trigger mode, the envelope ignores Note Off.

Envelope Beat/Sync Rate (Repeat) — The envelope will be retriggered after this amount of beat-time, as long as it is still on. When retriggered, the envelope will move at the given attack rate from the current level to the peak level.

Envelope Loop Time (Time) — If a note is still on after the end of the decay/sustain segment, the envelope will start again from its initial value. The time it takes to move from the sustain level to the initial value is defined by this parameter.

quotes.quote: Engines A and B each have a selection of twenty-four oscillator types to choose from, including six scale aware oscillators marked with a (♭♯). These range from simple sine wave generation oscillators to layered wave swarms, complex frequency modulation, noise looping, and ambient sound generation algorithms. Oscillator Types can be selected from an engine’s drop-down menu or cycled through using the arrows in the Oscillator Types displays.

The Swarm Sine, Swarm Triangle, Swarm Saw, and Swarm Square oscillators have two macro knobs, Motion and Spacing. Motion adds modulation to the wave swarm being produced. Spacing fades between increasingly complex chords as the amount applied is increased.

The Chord oscillator layers four sawtooth oscillators to create a variety of chords. It has two macro knobs, Shape and Inversion. Shape defines the intervals between the notes in the chord, while Inversion rearranges the order of the notes. When the Use Current Scale toggle is enabled in the device title bar, generated chords use the notes of the set scale. If no scale is set, a major scale is used with the incoming MIDI note as the root.

When Oscillator Scale Awareness is activated, pitches controlled by scale-aware oscillator types will also be in scale. The following oscillator types, marked with a (♭♯), are scale aware: Dual Basic Shapes, Swarm Sine, Swarm Triangle, Swarm Saw, Swarm Square, and Chip.

When Filter Scale Awareness is enabled, the resonating frequencies of scale-aware filter types will also be in scale. The following filter types, marked with a (♭♯), are scale aware: Plate Resonator and Membrane Resonator.

quotes.quote: Modulation sources are listed horizontally and modulation targets are listed vertically. Click and drag a cell up or down to apply modulation between parameters. Negative values will make envelopes and LFOs faster and positive values will make them slower. Note that some parameters have additive modulation applied to them, while others have multiplicative modulation applied to them.
Additive modulation is applied to a parameter using the following formula:
The outputs of a parameter’s modulation sources are summed together.
Multiplicative modulation is applied to a parameter using the following formula:
The outputs of a parameter’s modulation sources are multiplied together.

The Time slider will scale the times of all the modulators. Negative values will make envelopes and LFOs faster, while positive values will make them slower. Modulating this value with an envelope or LFO will not affect the assigned modulator, but that modulator will still scale to other destinations.

quotes.quote: Retrigger (R) — When enabled, notes that are enabled will be retriggered, rather than generating an additional voice.
These modulation targets are available as MIDI routing destinations in the global display, and also as modulation targets for the LFO and pitch envelope.
Filter Frequency — Modulates the cutoff frequency of the filter.
Filter Q (Legacy) — Modulates the resonance of the filter when using the legacy filter types.

quotes.quote: You can apply one of nine playback effects to further sculpt a sample’s sound: Stretch, Loop, Pitch Env, Punch, 8-Bit, FM, Ring Mod, Sub Osc, and Noise.

Noise Osc layers a noise oscillator with the sample. The Noise Amount knob sets the oscillator’s level. The oscillator envelope uses the device’s attack and decay settings. The Noise Color control sets the frequency used to filter the oscillator.
You can modulate any of the individual envelope stages with the Attack, Hold, and Decay targets.

quotes.quote: Wavetable’s oscillators have been optimized for maximum sound quality. As long as no modulation is applied, the raw output of the oscillators is perfectly band-limited and will not produce aliasing artifacts at any pitch.

You can extend the sonic capabilities of Wavetable’s oscillator section by loading any WAV or AIFF file as a wavetable. To do this, drag and drop a sample from the browser directly onto the wavetable visualization. The choosers and arrow buttons will now reference the folder containing the imported sample, allowing you to quickly audition any other samples in that folder.

Wavetable will automatically process imported samples to reduce unwanted artefacts. Note that you can bypass this processing by activating the Raw mode switch. Raw mode is especially useful when loading files that have been prepared specifically for use as a wavetable. However, it can also be “misused” to create unpredictable, noisy or glitchy sounds.
You can toggle on Hi-Quality mode on or off from Wavetable’s context menu.
When Hi-Quality is off, Wavetable modulation is calculated every 32 samples. Low-power versions of the Cytomic filters are also used to further reduce CPU.
Using Wavetable with Hi-Quality mode off can save up to 25% CPU compared to having it enabled, which is ideal for working with large sets or maintaining low latencies.

As of Live 11.1, Hi-Quality mode will be off by default when loading a new instance of Wavetable or any of its Core Library presets. However, any user presets or Live Sets created previously will still load Wavetable in Hi-Quality mode to ensure sound consistency with earlier Live versions.
Note: Subtle sound differences may occur when Hi-Quality mode is enabled.

quotes.quote: The Transpose slider lets you adjust the global pitch in semitones within a range of -48 to 48 st. You can switch on the Note PB toggle to enable per-note pitch bend. Switching Note PB off lets you use an MPE controller without having the pitch change based on finger position. The PB Range slider sets the global pitch bend range in semitones.
Enable Per-Note Pitch Bend — This option allows Drum Sampler to receive per-note pitch bend messages and is enabled by default.

Enable Per-Note Pitch Bend — This option is enabled by default so that Operator responds to per-note pitch bend changes. If needed, you can deactivate this behavior by deselecting the option in the device title bar’s context menu.

Pitch Bend, Press, and Modulation Wheel are hardware controls found on many MIDI controller devices. Note Pitch Bend, Slide, and Press are hardware controls found on many MPE controller devices. If you don’t have a MIDI or MPE controller, you can still modulate these parameters using clip envelopes.
